reasons.specificity: The analysis tracks Weber's role text by text across all 27 supplied sources, distinguishes coauthored from sole-authored texts, separates five Weber works by section title and page, labels moves as evidence/foil/dialogue/genealogy per text, and identifies specific loci (E&S 917, 919, 965-66, 1028-31, 1407-10; MWG A180; FMW 126, 194; Methodology 172). It also identifies secondary-reader mediations (Gorski, Judt, Biernacki, Runciman, Brown) as distinct from direct engagement. This specificity is genuine and grounded in the supplied sources rather than generic Weber-reception themes.
reasons.anchoring: Most quoted anchors appear verbatim in the supplied sources and support the interpretations attributed to them: 'Following in this Gramscian and Weberian tradition' (BEFGGK6M), 'Adapting Weber's concept of Roman imperialist capitalism' (CX58SV9M), 'When workers organise in this second way they do not form a class, they form what Max Weber called an estate' (QKSXS3VW), 'Marx approached capitalism from the standpoint of wage labour, Weber from that of the owners of capital' (9Z9GMMNI), 'the ethic of responsibility was embodied by the political actor who took responsibility for the use of legitimate violence' (H6GGBV9I). Some anchors support narrower claims than the analysis asserts: the PSYPHAPS citation-stance row was correctly marked 'no relevant instance' in scope records but the prose still presents a qualified adoption stance; and several 'builds on' labels rely on surrounding inference rather than explicit passage predicates. The F-tag system is useful but the scope records are heavily marked inconclusive, limiting certification.
reasons.non_obviousness: Several distinctions a casual reader would miss are drawn and supported: (1) Weber 1922 p.180 is marginal A180 in MWG I/23, not printed MWG p.180—correctly flagged and source-consistent; (2) Riley does not fuse closure, status honour, and estate—the analysis explicitly refuses the planning memo's fusion thesis with textual warrant; (3) the 2013 Routes or Rivals citation-stance is correctly assessed as 'no relevant instance' (mere reporting) while the broader prose captures the intellectual engagement; (4) secondary-reader mediations (Gorski, Biernacki, Brown) are systematically distinguished from direct Weber use; (5) the 'Einkesselung' framing in Angles of Vision is identified as a Lukácsian enclosure that preserves rather than dismisses Weber; (6) the modal hedge 'adapting... this could perhaps be termed' in Faultlines is noted as important, not elided.
reasons.coherence: The passage×object×move×stance×reading×locus table, the trajectory table, and the prose findings ledger are largely consistent with each other and with the supplied sources. Coauthorship is preserved in the tables. The scope-assessment appendix consistently uses 'inconclusive' rather than false positives. One internal tension: the prose treatment of PSYPHAPS attributes a 'qualified adoption' of Weber's material imperialism thesis, but the scope records correctly record 'no relevant instance' for citation_stance because no single anchor carries an explicit stance predicate—the analysis should have flagged this tension more clearly rather than presenting both interpretations without reconciliation.
reasons.usefulness: The five 'read first' recommendations are well-chosen and justified: What Is Trump (hybrid domination application), Routes or Rivals (political capitalism genesis), Reflections on Brown (deepest critical reconstruction), Rise of Political Capitalism (estate/class distinction), Angles of Vision (final Marxist enclosure). The passage×move×stance table gives a scholar actionable entry points with loci. The trajectory table is honest about ordering uncertainty for same-year texts and the undated essay. The unsettled question about suturing estate and class politics is genuinely open. Coverage of all 27 texts is attempted with appropriate scope qualifications. The analysis is usable as a reading guide.
reasons.hallucination_risk: No fabricated Weber quotations are introduced. The MWG A180 edition note is correctly derived from the supplied check metadata. The Hobson-Lenin proximity claim is presented as Riley's reading, not a certified Weber position. Coauthorship is preserved throughout. The 2005 German MWG edition mismatch with the cited English Methodology is noted correctly. One small risk: the prose says 'Riley quotes' the conviction/responsibility supplements passage from Judt as coming from Weber, but the supplied source says 'from Max Weber: Essays in Sociology, Hans Gerth, ed., Oxford 1958'—the footnote establishes the edition is 1958 while the held copy is 1948, and this edition caution from the metadata is noted in the scope records but slightly underemphasized in the main prose. No invented scholarly consensus, false absence claims, or invented citations detected.

score.one_line: A well-anchored, source-specific bibliographic reading that correctly identifies Weber's variable roles across 27 texts, preserves coauthorship and edition limits, and offers actionable read-first guidance, with one underresolved tension between the PSYPHAPS prose treatment and its own scope-record finding.
